days.title: Your First Build
days.theme: Start building your chosen project. Day one of your specialist track. Write your first line of real code.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

Today you write your first real line of code for your project. Not a tutorial. Not someone else's exercise. Yours. It will probably be small — a webpage that shows your project's title, a script that prints "hello world", a Notion template that structures your data. It doesn't matter how small. What matters is that it exists and it didn't yesterday. The first build is always the hardest because the blank page is the enemy. Today you defeat the blank page.
days.whyItMatters: Every substantial thing ever built started with one line. The emotional barrier to the first commit is real. Getting over it today means everything else is iteration — and iteration is just practice.
days.buildTask: Open your code editor (VS Code is recommended — download free at code.visualstudio.com). Create your project folder. Write the first file. For web builders: an index.html with your project's name and a one-sentence description. For backend builders: a main.py or index.js that prints your project idea to the terminal. For agent builders: a Zapier workflow with your first trigger. Run it. See something happen. Share a screenshot on WhatsApp with the words: "Day 37. It exists."
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

You wrote your first file. Now ask AI to review it and suggest the next three files or components you should build to get to a working prototype. Pick one of the three, build it today. Then come back and ask AI again. This is the loop: build the smallest next thing, show it to AI, get the next move. You're not planning ahead five steps — you're always one step ahead of yourself. That rhythm is how solo builders ship.
days.reflectionPrompt: What was the hardest part of starting — and what finally got you to do it?

days.title: React, Node, Python — Demystified
days.theme: What each language and framework actually does. When to use what. Stop being intimidated by the jargon.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

The words React, Node.js, and Python are everywhere. Here is what they actually mean. Python is a programming language — readable, beginner-friendly, excellent for AI, data, and backend logic. Node.js is a way of running JavaScript on a server, not just in a browser — used heavily for backends and APIs. React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces — the thing that makes websites interactive and dynamic. They are not competitors. They are different tools for different layers of your project. You don't need to master all three. You need to know which one your project needs and why.
days.whyItMatters: Half the intimidation of tech is vocabulary. When you understand what these words actually mean — and when you'd use each one — the landscape stops being a wall and starts being a map.
days.buildTask: Ask any AI: "Based on this project description: [describe yours], which of React, Node.js, or Python would I need — and why? What would each one do in my specific project? Which should I start with?" Then look at your first file from yesterday and ask AI to explain every line. Share the explanation that surprised you most on WhatsApp.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

You know what language your project uses. Now write a function in it — the most useful small function your project needs. Something that takes an input and returns an output. Ask AI to walk you through writing it step by step, explaining every line as you go. Don't copy-paste. Type it yourself. Then break it intentionally — delete a bracket, misspell a variable. Read the error. Ask AI what the error means. Learning to read errors is the most underrated programming skill, and you just practised it on purpose.
days.reflectionPrompt: Which technology in your stack feels most foreign — and what's your plan to get comfortable with it?

days.title: Frontend vs Backend
days.theme: What happens in the browser vs on the server. The invisible architecture behind every app you use.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

Frontend is everything the user sees and touches — the layout, the buttons, the colours, the text on screen. It lives in the browser. Backend is everything that happens before the user sees anything — the logic, the calculations, the data retrieval, the authentication. It lives on a server. Most apps need both. A login form is frontend. Checking if the password is correct is backend. The result — "welcome back" or "wrong password" — travels from backend to frontend and appears on screen. Understanding where things live helps you build them in the right place.
days.whyItMatters: When something breaks, knowing whether it's a frontend or backend problem tells you where to look. When you're designing a feature, knowing which layer handles which job makes the build faster and cleaner.
days.buildTask: Build something that has both layers — even simply. For web builders: a form in HTML (frontend) that when submitted, logs the data to the console (the simplest possible backend response). For others: ask AI to describe the frontend and backend of your specific project in detail. Share the diagram or description on WhatsApp.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

You built a form today. Now make it do something useful — specifically for your project. What is the first piece of data your project needs to collect from a user? Build that form. Give every field a real label. Add a submit button. Then ask AI: "What should happen on the backend when this form is submitted? Walk me through the logic step by step." You're not just learning frontend and backend as concepts — you're connecting them to something real that needs to exist.
days.reflectionPrompt: In your project, what decisions belong to the frontend and what belongs to the backend — and where is the boundary?

days.title: APIs: How Things Talk to Each Other
days.theme: APIs are how software communicates. Call one, receive data, display it. Your project connects to the world.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

You've heard the word API many times now. Today you call one. An API is a door that a service opens so that other software can talk to it. When your weather app shows you today's forecast, it called a weather API. When a website lets you log in with Google, it called Google's authentication API. Calling an API means sending a request — "give me the weather for Mumbai" — and receiving a response — a JSON object with temperature, humidity, conditions. JSON is just structured data. Once you've called one API and seen the response, APIs stop being abstract.
days.whyItMatters: Almost every interesting thing you'll build will talk to at least one API. Your project almost certainly needs one — whether it's an AI API, a data API, or a service API. Getting comfortable with the request-response cycle today means you can connect your project to the world's data.
days.buildTask: Call a free public API with no authentication required. Go to https://api.github.com/users/your-username in your browser — you'll see JSON data about a GitHub profile. Then use AI to write a small Python or JavaScript snippet that calls this API and prints the user's name and location. Run it. Share the output on WhatsApp.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

You called a public API. Now call the one your project actually needs. Find the API documentation for the service you identified in your reflection prompt. Look for a free tier or sandbox. Ask AI: "Help me make my first API call to [service] using [your language]. Show me the request, the expected response, and how to extract the data I need." Run it. Even if the response is just raw JSON on screen, you've made the connection. Your project just touched the internet.
days.reflectionPrompt: Which API would make your project ten times more useful if you could connect to it — and what data would it give you?

days.title: Debugging With AI
days.theme: When your code breaks, AI is your pair programmer. How to describe errors, read stack traces, fix fast.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

Your code will break. This is not failure — it is the job. Debugging is the process of finding and fixing what broke. Without AI, debugging meant searching Stack Overflow for hours, reading documentation, and guessing. With AI, debugging looks like this: copy the error message, paste it into Claude or ChatGPT, describe what you were trying to do, and ask what went wrong. Nine times out of ten, you get the answer in thirty seconds. The skill is not avoiding errors — it's reading them clearly enough to ask the right question.
days.whyItMatters: Developers who are fast are not the ones who write perfect code. They are the ones who debug fast. AI has collapsed the time between "something broke" and "I know why" from hours to minutes. This is one of the biggest productivity unlocks of the AI era for builders.
days.buildTask: Intentionally break something in your project — remove a semicolon, misname a variable, delete a bracket. Read the error message carefully. Then paste the error and your code into any AI tool and ask: "What is wrong and how do I fix it?" Compare what AI said to what you thought the problem was. Share the error, the AI diagnosis, and whether it was right on WhatsApp.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

You debugged one error. Now build your personal error log. Every time your project breaks from today until Day 66, write one line: what broke, what the error said, how you fixed it. Keep it in a Notion page or a text file. At the end of the week, paste the log into AI and ask: "What patterns do you see in my errors? What should I learn or change about how I'm writing code?" Your error log is the most honest record of what you're actually learning.
days.reflectionPrompt: What's the difference between an error you could diagnose yourself and one where you genuinely needed AI?

days.title: Databases 101
days.theme: Where data lives. Tables, rows, queries. Connect your project to a simple database and watch it remember things.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

A database is where your application remembers things. Without a database, every time a user closes your app, everything is gone. With a database, you can store users, posts, responses, records — and retrieve them later. The simplest mental model: a database is a collection of tables. A table is like a spreadsheet — rows and columns. Each row is a record. Each column is a field. SQL is the language you use to talk to a relational database. If your project needs to store anything that persists — sign-ups, submissions, content — it needs a database.
days.whyItMatters: Most projects get stuck not because the frontend or backend is hard, but because the builder didn't think about data early enough. Knowing where your data lives and how it's structured before you build saves you from redesigning everything halfway through.
days.buildTask: Set up a free Supabase account at supabase.com. Create a new project. Create one table that your project needs — for example, a users table with columns for name, email, and sign-up date. Use the Supabase interface, not code. Add three fake rows of data. Share a screenshot of your table on WhatsApp.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

You created a table manually. Now connect it to your project with code. Ask AI: "Show me how to connect my [Python/JavaScript] project to Supabase and insert one row into my [table name] table." Run the code. Check Supabase — is the row there? You just made your project write to a real database. Now ask AI to show you how to read it back. You've just completed the full data cycle: create, write, read. Everything else is variation on this loop.
days.reflectionPrompt: What data does your project need to store — and what happens to your project if that data disappears?

days.title: Reflection: Week 6
days.theme: What's working? What broke? Share your build progress and one thing that surprised you.
days.lesson:
This week's arc:

You built something. It might be small. It might be rough. It might have broken three times. But it exists — and it didn't a week ago. You wrote code, called an API, set up a database, debugged with AI, and started to understand the difference between what happens in the browser and what happens on the server. That is a week most people never have.
days.whyItMatters: Next week is Shipping. You'll learn Git, GitHub, and how to deploy your project so it lives on the internet and not just your laptop. By Sunday, your project will have a URL. Real, public, shareable. See you Monday.
days.buildTask:
Your Week 6 wins — take five minutes and write down:

1. What your project can do today that it couldn't on Monday
2. The most useful AI debugging moment this week
3. What you're building next week — specifically
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

Reflection day is also code review day. Paste your most important file into AI and ask: "Review this code. What works well? What would a more experienced developer change? What's the most fragile part?" Then make one improvement based on the feedback — just one. Not a rewrite. One targeted fix. This is how real code improves: weekly reviews, small improvements, compounding quality. Your codebase is a week old. Start treating it like something worth maintaining.
days.reflectionPrompt:
Post one of these today:

"Here's what my project looks like after Week 6: [screenshot or description]. Here's what's next."

"The moment this week when building clicked for me was _."

"I got stuck on __ and got unstuck by __."

days.title: What is Git?
days.theme: Version control. The safety net every builder needs. Commit, push, pull — the language of shipping.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

Git is a version control system. That means it tracks every change you make to your code over time — who changed what, when, and why. Think of it as a time machine for your project. If you break something, you can go back. If you want to try something risky, you create a branch — a parallel version of your project — experiment, and merge it back if it works or delete it if it doesn't. Every professional developer uses Git. Every serious project lives in Git. Today you start using it too.
days.whyItMatters: Without Git, a single bad change can destroy hours of work. With Git, nothing is ever truly lost. It is the safety net that lets you build boldly — because you know you can always go back.
days.buildTask: Install Git at git-scm.com if you haven't already. Open your terminal, navigate to your project folder, and run three commands: git init (start tracking), git add . (stage all your files), git commit -m "Day 44 — first commit" (save a snapshot). Share a screenshot of your terminal showing the commit confirmation on WhatsApp.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

You made your first commit. Now make Git part of your daily habit. From today until Day 66, commit every time you complete something meaningful — not every line, but every working chunk. Write commit messages that describe what you built, not just "update" or "fix". At the end of each day, run git log and read your own history. Ask AI: "Based on these commit messages, am I making consistent progress? What does my build velocity look like?" Your commit history is your most honest progress diary.
days.reflectionPrompt: What would you have lost from your project this week if you hadn't had the ability to go back in time?

days.title: GitHub Basics
days.theme: Your project lives on GitHub. Create a repo, push your code, share it with the world.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

Git lives on your laptop. GitHub lives on the internet. GitHub is where you push your Git repository — your code and its history — so it's backed up, shareable, and deployable. A repository is simply a project folder that Git is tracking. When you push your repo to GitHub, it becomes accessible from anywhere. Other people can see it (if it's public), collaborate on it, and tools like Vercel can read it to deploy your project automatically. GitHub is where code goes to live.
days.whyItMatters: Your laptop can break. GitHub doesn't. Every project you ever build should live on GitHub. It's your portfolio, your backup, and your deployment gateway — all in one place.
days.buildTask: Create a free account at github.com. Create a new repository called she-vibes-project. Connect your local project to it using: git remote add origin [your repo URL] then git push -u origin main. Refresh GitHub in your browser — you should see your code there. Share the GitHub link on WhatsApp. Your code is now on the internet.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

Your code is on GitHub. Now write a proper README for it. A README is the first thing anyone sees when they visit your repository. Ask AI: "Write a README for my project: [describe it]. Include what it does, who it's for, how to run it locally, and what's coming next." Push the README to GitHub. Now your project has a face. This is also the beginning of your public portfolio — the record of what you built during She Vibes that will exist long after June 9th.
days.reflectionPrompt: What does it mean to you that your project is now publicly visible — even in its early, rough form?

days.title: Deploying Your First Project
days.theme: From laptop to the internet. Deploy on Vercel, Netlify, or Railway. Watch your project go live.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

Deployment is the act of making your project accessible to anyone in the world — not just you, not just your laptop, but anyone with a browser and a URL. Until now, your project has lived on localhost. Local means private. Deployment means public. When you deploy, your code is copied to a server somewhere in the world — a computer that runs 24/7, connected to the internet, ready to serve your project to anyone who asks. You don't need to own the server. You don't need to manage it. Tools like Vercel, Netlify, and Railway do all of that for you. You connect your GitHub repo, click a button, and your project gets a URL.

The three tools:

Vercel — built for frontend projects. Ideal for React, Next.js, or any static HTML/CSS/JS site. Connect your GitHub repo and every push to main automatically redeploys. Free tier is generous. This is the fastest path to a live URL.

Netlify — similar to Vercel. Great for static sites and simple backends. Has built-in form handling and serverless functions. Also free to start.

Railway — built for backend projects and databases. If your project has a Python Flask or Node.js server, or a PostgreSQL database, Railway is where it goes. Slightly more setup but handles full-stack projects that Vercel can't.
days.whyItMatters: A project that only lives on your laptop is invisible. A project with a URL is real. It exists in the world. It can be shared, tested, seen, and used. When someone asks what you built during She Vibes, you want to send them a link — not describe something that lives in a folder no one can open. Deployment is the difference between building something and shipping something. Most people never ship. Today you do.
days.buildTask: Go to vercel.com and create a free account. Connect your GitHub account. Click "New Project" and import the repository you created on Day 45. Vercel will detect your project type and deploy it automatically. In under two minutes, you will have a live URL. Open it. It's your project — on the internet. Share that URL on WhatsApp. That's your milestone for today.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

Your project is live. Now send the URL to someone outside the cohort — a friend, a family member, a colleague — and ask them to open it on their phone. Watch what breaks. Watch what works. Ask them one question: "What's the first thing you tried to do?" Then fix one thing based on what they showed you. This is called user testing. It is the fastest way to find problems that you've stopped seeing because you built the thing. Real users find things developers never notice. You just ran your first external test. Now push the fix and watch Vercel redeploy automatically.
days.reflectionPrompt: What did it feel like to open a URL and see something you built — live on the internet?

days.title: Domains and DNS
days.theme: Your project has a URL. What happens behind the scenes. Buy a domain, connect it, own your corner of the internet.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

Right now your project lives at a URL like she-vibes-project.vercel.app. That works — but it's not yours. A domain is an address you own. yourname.com, shevibes.in, whatever you choose. DNS — Domain Name System — is the system that translates that human-readable address into the IP address of the server where your project lives. Buying a domain costs about ₹800–1500 per year. Connecting it to Vercel takes five minutes. After that, your project has a home that belongs to you.
days.whyItMatters: Your project's domain is its identity. When you share it on LinkedIn or WhatsApp, a custom domain signals that this is real — not a side experiment. It's a small investment with a large signal.
days.buildTask: Go to Namecheap (namecheap.com) or GoDaddy. Search for a domain that fits your project — keep it short, memorable, and relevant. You don't have to buy it today. But price it, decide if it's worth it, and if yes — buy it and connect it to your Vercel project using their custom domain settings. Share your domain name — purchased or just decided — on WhatsApp.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

You have a domain or you've decided on one. Now think about your digital identity beyond this project. Ask AI: "Help me design a personal domain strategy. I want one domain that can house my portfolio, my current project, and future projects. What naming convention and subdomain structure would you recommend?" Your domain is not just for this project — it's the beginning of your public presence as a builder. Invest 20 minutes thinking about what you want that presence to say.
days.reflectionPrompt: What does having your own domain say about how seriously you take what you're building?

days.title: Environment Variables and Secrets
days.theme: API keys, passwords, secrets. How to keep them safe. The basics of production security every builder must know.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

Your project probably connects to at least one external service — an AI API, a database, an email provider. Each of these gives you a key — a secret string of characters that proves it's you making the request. These keys must never be put directly into your code. Why? Because your code lives on GitHub — and GitHub is public. If your API key is in your code, anyone can find it, use your account, and rack up charges. Environment variables are the safe way to store secrets: they live outside your code, in a configuration file or in your deployment platform's settings, and your code reads them without exposing them.
days.whyItMatters: API key leaks are one of the most common and costly mistakes junior builders make. Learning this now — before it matters — means you never make it.
days.buildTask: Create a .env file in your project root. Add one variable: MY_PROJECT_NAME="She Vibes". Add .env to your .gitignore file so it never gets pushed to GitHub. Then add the same variable in Vercel's Environment Variables settings. Ask AI: "Show me how to read an environment variable in [your language] and use it in my code." Share a screenshot showing the variable in Vercel — not the value, just the key name — on WhatsApp.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

You secured your secrets. Now do a full security audit of your project. Ask AI: "Review this project description: [describe yours]. What are the top five security risks I should know about for a project of this type? For each one, tell me how to prevent it." Then check your code against the list. Fix at least one thing. Security is not a feature you add later — it's a habit you build now, when the project is small and the fixes are easy.
days.reflectionPrompt: What secrets does your project currently have — and where are they stored right now?

days.title: Shipping is a Mindset
days.theme: Done is better than perfect. How to ship fast, iterate faster. The builder's relationship with the finish line.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

Done is not perfect. Done is live. The mindset shift that separates builders who ship from builders who polish forever is this: version one is supposed to be rough. Its job is not to impress — its job is to exist so that version two can be better. Every product you use started as something embarrassing. Twitter was a side project. Instagram launched with no DMs. Google was a Stanford research paper. The pattern is always the same: ship something real, watch how people use it, make it better. The loop only starts when you ship.
days.whyItMatters: Perfectionism is procrastination with better branding. The moment you decide your project is good enough to share — even if it's not good enough to be proud of — is the moment you become a builder.
days.buildTask: Make one improvement to your live project — fix one thing that bothers you, add one feature you've been putting off, improve one piece of copy. Commit it, push it to GitHub, watch Vercel redeploy automatically. That automatic redeploy — code to live in under two minutes — is the shipping superpower. Share what you changed and why on WhatsApp.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

You shipped an improvement today. Now write your project's public launch post — even if you're not ready to publish it. Describe what you built, why you built it, what problem it solves, and what you learned building it. Write it for LinkedIn or Twitter. Ask AI to review it for clarity and impact. Don't publish it yet if you're not ready. But having it written means shipping is one click away. The builders who announce publicly ship faster — because the announcement creates the accountability.
days.reflectionPrompt: What would "good enough to share" look like for your project — and are you there yet?

days.title: Reflection: Week 7
days.theme: Is your project live? Share the link. Celebrate what you shipped, even if it's small.
days.lesson:
This week's arc:

You shipped. Not someday. This week. Your project has a URL, a GitHub repository, a database, and environment variables that keep your secrets safe. You know what Git is, how deployment works, why domains matter, and how to push a change and watch it go live in under two minutes. Most people who say they want to build something never get here. You did.
days.whyItMatters:
Next week is Collaboration — the final foundation week. You'll learn how to work with other humans when AI is in the loop, how to review and own AI-generated code, and how to think about the ethics and responsibility of what you've built. Then it's Challenge Week. One week to build something end-to-end, ship it, and tell the world about it.

See you Monday.
days.buildTask:
Your Week 7 wins — take five minutes and write down:

1. Your live project URL — write it down somewhere permanent
2. One thing that broke during deployment and how you fixed it
3. What your project needs to be ready for the challenge week
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

Fifty days in. Do a full project retrospective. Open a blank doc and write three sections: what's working well, what's technically broken or rough, and what you would do differently if you started over. Then ask AI: "Based on this retrospective, what should I prioritise in my final two weeks to have the strongest possible project by Day 66?" A builder who reflects is a builder who compounds. Most people only look forward. The ones who look back get better faster.
days.reflectionPrompt:
Post one of these today:

"My project is live at [URL]. Here's what it does and what's still rough."
"The most satisfying moment this week was __ — because __."
"The thing I want to add in Week 8 before Challenge Week is _."

days.title: Building With Others
days.theme: How to work on the same codebase with another person. Branches, pull requests, code review basics.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

Most real software is built by more than one person. And the moment more than one person touches a codebase, you need structure. Git branches are how this works. Instead of everyone writing to the same file, each person works on their own branch — a parallel copy of the project — and merges their changes back when ready. A pull request is the formal act of saying "I've made changes, please review them before merging." Code review is someone else reading your code before it goes live. It catches bugs, spreads knowledge, and keeps quality high.
days.whyItMatters: Even if you're building solo right now, understanding branches and pull requests means you can collaborate on any open source project, bring someone else into your project, and operate like a professional from day one.
days.buildTask: Create a new branch in your project: git checkout -b day-51-experiment. Make one small change to your project on this branch. Commit it. Then create a pull request on GitHub — even if you're merging it yourself. Write a description of what you changed and why. Merge it. Share a screenshot of your merged pull request on WhatsApp.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

You created and merged a branch. Now find one woman in the cohort whose project interests you and ask her to review one file from your project — not as a developer, but as a user or a reader. Share the file, ask her: what is unclear, what feels fragile, what question does it leave unanswered? Then do the same for her. You've just done your first human code review. The combination of AI review and human review is the highest-quality feedback loop available to a solo builder.
days.reflectionPrompt: What would change about how you build if you knew someone else would always read your code before it shipped?

days.title: Communicating Your Architecture
days.theme: How to explain what you built and why. Diagrams, documentation, readme files. The builder as communicator.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

A builder who can't explain what they've built is only half a builder. The other half is communication — the ability to describe your architecture clearly to someone who wasn't there when you made the decisions. A README is the front door of your project: what it does, why it exists, how to set it up, and how to contribute. A diagram shows how the pieces fit together. Good documentation is not a nice-to-have — it is the difference between a project that lives and one that dies the moment you stop working on it.
days.whyItMatters: When you explain your project clearly, three things happen: you find the gaps in your own thinking, others can contribute, and your project becomes shareable — on LinkedIn, in job applications, in funding conversations. Documentation is how your work speaks when you're not in the room.
days.buildTask: Write a README for your project. Include: what it does in one sentence, who it's for, how to set it up from scratch, what technologies it uses, and what you're planning to add next. Commit it to your GitHub repository as README.md. Share your GitHub link on WhatsApp — the README is now the first thing people see when they visit.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

Your README explains your project. Now draw its architecture diagram and add it to the README. Use any tool — Excalidraw, Figma, even a photograph of a paper sketch. Show the frontend, backend, database, and any external APIs. Label the arrows. Ask AI: "Review this architecture diagram description: [describe it]. Is it accurate? What's missing? What would a senior developer ask about this design?" A project with a clear diagram gets taken more seriously than one without. It shows you understand what you built.
days.reflectionPrompt: If someone found your project on GitHub right now with no context, what would they understand — and what would confuse them?

referenceLinks.text: How to write a great README — makeareadme.com

days.title: AI in the Team
days.theme: Working with humans when AI is also in the loop. When to show your AI-assisted work and how to own it.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

When AI is part of how you build, collaboration gets more complicated. Your teammate might not know which parts of the code AI wrote and which parts you did. Your manager might not know how much of the output was AI-assisted. Your client might not know that the design was generated. None of this is inherently wrong — but it requires intentionality. The norm emerging in the best teams is transparency: you say which parts AI helped with, you take responsibility for all of it, and you use AI to raise the floor, not to hide the ceiling.
days.whyItMatters: Trust in collaborative work is built on honesty. The builders and teams that will earn lasting trust are the ones who are clear about how they work — not the ones who pretend AI didn't help. Owning your AI-assisted work is a mark of confidence, not a confession.
days.buildTask: Write a short personal policy for yourself — one paragraph — on how you'll use AI in collaborative work. When will you disclose it? How will you ensure you understand what AI built for you? What will you always do yourself? Share it on WhatsApp. It doesn't have to be perfect. It just has to be honest.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

You wrote your personal AI policy. Now take it to your actual workplace. Look at one real project or deliverable you're currently collaborating on with others. Ask yourself: where am I using AI in this work, and have I been transparent about it? Draft a message to your team or manager that introduces how you're working with AI — not defensively, but confidently. Ask AI to help you write it. The act of using AI to communicate your AI use policy is the most meta, and most honest, thing you can do today.
days.reflectionPrompt: What would you want to know if someone on your team was using AI to contribute to a shared project?

referenceLinks.text: Co-Intelligence: Living and Working with AI — Ethan Mollick

days.title: Reviewing AI-Generated Code
days.theme: You're responsible for what AI writes. How to read, understand, and take ownership of AI-generated code.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

AI can write code faster than you can read it. That speed is the trap. When you copy AI-generated code without understanding it, you own the output but not the knowledge. If it breaks, you don't know why. If it has a security flaw, you shipped it. If someone asks you to explain it, you can't. The rule is simple: never ship code you can't explain. This doesn't mean you write every line yourself — it means you read every line, you ask AI to explain what you don't understand, and you take responsibility for what goes live under your name.
days.whyItMatters: The value of a builder is not the ability to generate code. It's the ability to make good decisions about code. AI handles the generation. You handle the judgment. That judgment is yours and it cannot be delegated.
days.buildTask: Pick a piece of AI-generated code in your project — a function, a component, a script. Read it line by line. For every line you don't fully understand, ask AI: "Explain this line to me. What does it do? Why is it written this way? Are there any risks?" Keep asking until you can explain the whole thing yourself. Share the most interesting thing you learned on WhatsApp.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

You explained one piece of AI code today. Now do a full ownership audit of your project. Go through every file. Mark each function or component: green if you fully understand it, yellow if you mostly do, red if you couldn't explain it under pressure. Then take your red items back to AI one by one and work through them until they're green. Your goal before Day 66: no red in your codebase. A project you fully understand is a project you can confidently present, defend, and extend.
days.reflectionPrompt: What would you do differently in your project if you knew you'd have to explain every line of code in a live interview?

referenceLinks.text: How I use LLMs to help me write code — Simon Willison

days.title: Ethics in the Wild
days.theme: Privacy, bias, misuse. Real questions builders face. Not hypothetical — things that will show up in your work.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

Ethics in building is not abstract. It shows up in specific, practical decisions. Does your app collect data it doesn't need? Does it work for people with disabilities? Does it make assumptions about users based on their gender, location, or language? Does it give AI the ability to make decisions that affect people's lives without human review? These are not philosophy questions — they are design questions. And they have answers. The best builders ask them early, not after something goes wrong.
days.whyItMatters: As AI makes building faster and more accessible, the responsibility to build thoughtfully falls on more people. You are now one of those people. What you build matters. The choices you make in design and data have consequences in the real world.
days.buildTask: Audit your project for three things: data privacy (what data are you collecting and do you need it all?), accessibility (can someone using a screen reader or a slow phone use your project?), and bias (does your project make any assumptions about who the user is?). Ask AI to help: "Audit my project description for privacy, accessibility, and bias issues. Be specific." Share your most important finding on WhatsApp.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

You audited your project. Now write a public ethics statement for it — a short paragraph on your project's homepage or README that tells users how their data is handled, what AI does in your product, and what decisions are still made by humans. Ask AI to draft it, then rewrite it in your own voice. Publishing an ethics statement is rare at the indie builder level. It immediately signals that you build with intention. It also holds you accountable to it — which is the point.
days.reflectionPrompt: What is the most ethically significant decision you've made in your project — and would you make it the same way now?

days.title: The Builder's Responsibility
days.theme: What you build, you own. Impact, consequences, and the mindset of a conscious builder in the AI era.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

You have spent seven weeks learning to build. You can now create things that didn't exist before. Things that other people will use, interact with, rely on. That is power — and power without reflection is careless. The builder's responsibility is this: think about impact before you ship, not after. Who will use this? Who could misuse it? What happens if it breaks? What happens if it works exactly as designed — is that still good? The best builders hold these questions alongside the technical ones. Not to slow down, but to build better.
days.whyItMatters: The world will remember what people built with AI in this era. The question is not whether you built something impressive — it's whether you built something worth building. You get to decide that. Every day. Starting now.
days.buildTask: Write your builder's manifesto — a short, personal statement of what you commit to as someone who now builds with AI. Three to five sentences. What do you stand for? What will you never build? What will you always check before you ship? Share it on WhatsApp. Read everyone else's. This is who your cohort is.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

You wrote your manifesto. Now find one person in your life — outside the cohort — who is not technical and share it with them. Ask them: does this make you trust me as a builder? What would you add? What would you question? The people most affected by what builders make are often the least consulted. This conversation is a small act of that correction. Report back what you heard.
days.reflectionPrompt: Eight weeks ago you came in overwhelmed. What kind of builder do you want to be — and what does that mean about what you'll do next?

referenceLinks.text: Technology is Not Neutral — Stephanie Hare

These are not soft skills. They are the skills that determine whether you build things that last and things that matter.
